summary: Defines MIB objects for configuring, monitoring, and controlling network devices with APPC (Advanced Program-to-Program Communications) capabilities, using SNMPv2.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a control panel for managing machines that use an older IBM way for programs to talk to each other.

questions: what does the appc mib manage
subtitle: SNMP objects for monitoring and controlling IBM SNA APPC (LU 6.2) systems.

tldr.problem: Devices that run APPC, the peer-to-peer part of IBM's SNA, needed a standard SNMP view so that management stations could configure-check, monitor and control them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the APPC-MIB module with six groups of objects for global controls, local and partner LUs, modes, transaction programs, sessions, conversations and CPI-C side information, using paired Admin and Oper tables.
tldr.outcome: A manager can read LU 6.2 state, switch statistics and tracing on or off, issue CNOS session-limit commands and deactivate sessions. It cannot create or edit definitions or send traps.
tldr.outcomeLabel: What it can and cannot do

today: RFC 2051 is a Proposed Standard published in October 1996, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 2051 defines a portion of the MIB for managing the configuration, monitoring and controlling of network devices with APPC (Advanced Program-to-Program Communications) capabilities. It identifies managed objects for the SNA LU6.2 protocols. It uses the SMI and related documents (RFC 1902, RFC 1903, RFC 1904) to describe and name objects.

APPC is the part of SNA that supports peer-to-peer communication and gives applications their interface. The document covers both dependent LU 6.2 (which needs an SSCP to activate a session) and independent LU 6.2 (which does not). If an agent supports dependent LU 6.2 only, the SNA NAU MIB (RFC 1666) is used instead.
sections.plainLanguage: APPC is how programs on IBM's older network system talk to each other as equals. This document gives them a standard control panel that management tools can read.

sections.title: APPC Concepts the MIB Models
sections.content:
Local LUs and partner LUs connect to each other through sessions. Many sessions can exist between a pair, with characteristics defined by Modes. Session limits inside a mode are negotiated between the two LUs with a protocol called CNOS (Change Number of Sessions).

Transaction Programs (TPs) are the applications that use sessions. Several TPs can use the same session, but not at the same time. One use of a session is a conversation: a session may last a long time while conversations come and go. Common Programming Interface - Communications (CPI-C) is the standard API that TPs use to reach conversations. Many CPI-C objects are relevant to OSI TP as well, but the MIB intends to manage APPC products only.

The overall SNA and APPC architecture is documented in IBM references cited by the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: Two programs open a phone line (a session) and then have short chats on it (conversations). Rules called modes say what kind of line it is and how many lines are allowed.

sections.title: Structure of the Module
sections.content:
The module holds six groups: appcGlobal (global defaults and controls, plus CNOS), appcLu (local and partner LUs and modes), appcTp (transaction programs), appcSession (LU 6.2 sessions), appcConversation and appcCPIC (CPI-C side information).

Most LU 6.2 objects come in two kinds of table. An Admin table holds read-only default or expected configuration values; the MIB does not create or modify configuration. An Oper table holds current operational values such as state and negotiated parameters. Dynamic objects are created by the APPC system from Admin templates. Admin and Oper entries can drift apart: an implementation might let a mode definition be deleted while an active session still uses it.

Where definitions can apply to every local LU, the LU name column is set to *ALL. There is no Oper table for TPs, because that information tends to be product specific and can be derived from the conversation tables. Session tables include active sessions, session statistics, history of abnormally terminated sessions, and sessions carried over APPN High Performance Routing.
sections.plainLanguage: For many things there are two lists: one says how a thing was meant to be set up, the other says what is actually happening right now. They can differ.

sections.title: Control and CNOS Commands
sections.content:
The management functions include switching statistics keeping and tracing on and off, issuing CNOS commands, monitoring LU, mode, TP and CPI-C parameters, deactivating sessions, and monitoring session and conversation data. The control objects are optional, for agents that provide that level of control. The Admin group holds the desired state and the Oper group the actual state.

The appcCnosCommand object issues one of three CNOS commands: initSesslimit, changeSesslimit or resetSesslimit. The manager first sets the parameter objects that apply to the command, then the three target objects (local LU name, partner LU name and mode name), and finally sets appcCnosCommand itself to make the agent issue the command.

The MIB does not support modifying APPC defaults, creating or deleting partner LUs, modes, TPs or CPI-C side information, activating or deactivating LUs, conversations or TPs, activating sessions, or traps.
sections.plainLanguage: To change how many lines are allowed, you fill in the form first, say who it is for, and only then press the send button.

sections.title: How SNA Names Are Handled
sections.content:
SNA names (LU, CP, mode and COS names) may be padded with spaces in SNA formats, and those spaces are insignificant. The agent does not include them in values. A mode name of #INTER with a length of 6 is returned as length 6 with no spaces, however it appeared in the BIND RU. The only exception is the all-blank mode name, returned as eight spaces.

When a name is used as a table index, trailing spaces are significant. A request for a row with index #INTER does not match the row #INTER. The only reason for a manager to add spaces is to start GetNext processing at a chosen point, for example an 8-character index beginning with M.
sections.plainLanguage: Names in the old system may have invisible blank padding at the end. The panel hides it when showing a name, but when you look a name up it must match exactly.

sections.title: Compliance and Security
sections.content:
The compliance statement makes the global, local LU, partner LU, mode, TP and session groups unconditionally mandatory. Other groups are mandatory only for entities that implement the matching feature: control, CNOS, CPI-C, and conversation groups for session endpoints of non-control APPC sessions. Support for deactivating a session through appcActSessOperState is not required; it may be read-only.

The Security Considerations section has a single sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo. The long Definitions section is about 110 pages of object definitions and is not summarised object by object here.
sections.plainLanguage: A machine must have the main dials, and only needs the extra ones if it really has the matching feature. The document says nothing about safety.
